item.content:encoded:
The New York Times is offering a Local Investigations Fellowship, a one-year opportunity designed for experienced local reporters and freelance journalists who have compelling investigative story ideas focused on their state or region. The fellowship provides selected journalists with editorial guidance, investigative reporting training, resources and the opportunity to produce significant investigative journalism for publication by The New York Times.

The program is intended for journalists who have identified important local issues but may not have had sufficient time, resources or editorial support to pursue them fully. Fellows will work from the communities where they are reporting while receiving guidance from Dean Baquet, former executive editor of The New York Times, and a group of veteran investigative editors.

This opportunity is particularly relevant to journalists interested in accountability reporting, public-interest investigations, local government, public safety, health, community issues, institutional failures and other subjects where rigorous reporting can reveal information that has not previously been uncovered.

About The New York Times Local Investigations Fellowship

The New York Times describes its mission as seeking the truth and helping people understand the world, with independent journalism at the center of its work.

The Local Investigations Fellowship supports that mission by giving local journalists the opportunity to develop and pursue substantial investigative projects. Rather than simply providing a conventional newsroom position, the fellowship is structured around a specific investigative reporting idea or area of focus that the journalist wants to explore.

Successful fellows spend approximately one year working on investigative journalism focused on their state or region. Their work is expected to result in signature investigative reporting that will be published by The New York Times.

The fellowship combines practical reporting with editorial mentorship. Fellows remain based in the communities they cover, allowing them to maintain the local knowledge, relationships and sources needed for effective community-based investigative reporting. Periodic trips to The New York Times offices are also part of the program for training and support.

What the Local Investigations Fellowship Offers

The fellowship provides selected journalists with an opportunity to develop their investigative reporting skills while working on a substantial local story.

Key aspects of the fellowship include:

  • A one-year investigative reporting opportunity focused on a state or region.
  • The opportunity to produce signature investigative journalism for publication by The New York Times.
  • Editorial guidance from Dean Baquet, The New York Times’ former executive editor.
  • Support from a group of experienced investigative editors.
  • Training in the judgment, skills and techniques required for effective investigative journalism.
  • The opportunity to develop an investigation that may require significant reporting time, records, data and human sources.
  • Periodic travel to The New York Times offices for training and support.
  • The opportunity to bring new perspectives and approaches to investigative journalism.
  • The ability to work from the community where the reporting is taking place.

For journalists who have strong investigative ideas but have not had the resources or editorial support necessary to pursue them, the fellowship is structured to provide an environment in which those investigations can be developed in depth.

Who Can Apply for the Local Investigations Fellowship?

The fellowship is designed for experienced local journalists, including reporters currently working in local newsrooms and independent or freelance journalists.

Applicants must meet the basic professional requirements outlined by The New York Times.

Basic Qualifications

Applicants should have:

  • Three to five years of professional reporting experience covering a beat for a local newspaper or local digital news outlet.
  • Experience as either an independent journalist or a journalist employed by a newsroom that is willing to provide a yearlong sabbatical.
  • Authorization to work in the United States.

Applicants should also demonstrate an understanding of and commitment to journalistic independence and The New York Times’ mission of seeking the truth and helping people understand the world.

Preferred Qualifications

While not listed as mandatory, The New York Times identifies several qualities that can strengthen an application.

Preferred candidates may have:

  • Significant experience covering a particular reporting beat.
  • A well-developed investigative story idea that they have not previously had enough time, resources or editorial support to pursue.
  • The ability to bring new perspectives to investigative journalism.
  • A strong record of reporting stories that demonstrate excellence in writing, news judgment and community-centered journalism.

The fellowship is therefore aimed at journalists who already have professional reporting experience rather than individuals seeking their first journalism position.

What Kind of Investigative Story Is The New York Times Looking For?

A central part of the application is the investigative story idea.

Applicants are expected to propose an investigation that could reveal something important about their community, state or region. The proposed story should go beyond simply describing an existing problem. It should have the potential to uncover new information, establish accountability or reveal information that has not previously been made public.

The New York Times identifies several characteristics of a strong local investigation.

1. The Investigation Should Start With High Stakes

A compelling local investigation should address an issue that has meaningful consequences for people’s lives.

Applicants should consider questions such as:

  • How does the issue affect people’s health?
  • Does it affect public safety?
  • Does it threaten people’s livelihoods?
  • Does it affect access to essential services?
  • Does it affect people’s quality of life?
  • What are the consequences for the local community?

The strongest investigative ideas generally involve issues where the consequences are substantial and where uncovering the truth could make a meaningful difference to public understanding.

2. The Investigation Should Have a Clear Line of Accountability

A strong investigation should identify who has responsibility or power in relation to the issue being investigated.

Applicants should be able to explain:

  • Who is responsible for the situation?
  • What institution, organization or individual has decision-making authority?
  • What actions or failures contributed to the problem?
  • How can the investigation establish accountability?

The objective is not simply to identify a problem but to determine how responsibility can be traced through evidence and reporting.

3. The Investigation Should Reveal Something New

The fellowship places emphasis on investigations that uncover information that is not already known.

Applicants should consider whether their proposed investigation could:

  • Reveal previously unknown information.
  • Expose a hidden pattern.
  • Uncover records or data that have not been analyzed.
  • Demonstrate a previously undocumented failure.
  • Identify conduct or circumstances that institutions or individuals may not want publicly examined.
  • Provide evidence that changes understanding of an existing local issue.

Applicants are encouraged to explain what they believe their investigation could establish and why their reporting could reveal something that existing coverage has not.

4. The Investigation Should Have a Clear Sense of Place

Because this is a local investigations fellowship, the proposed investigation should have a strong connection to a particular community.

The applicant should be able to explain how the issue is connected to their state, city, region or local community and why the circumstances are distinctive there.

The local context could involve:

  • Local government.
  • Public institutions.
  • Health systems.
  • Schools and education.
  • Law enforcement.
  • Courts and the justice system.
  • Housing.
  • Environmental issues.
  • Public infrastructure.
  • Local businesses and industries.
  • Community organizations.
  • Public safety.
  • Local economic conditions.

The important point is that the investigation should have a meaningful local dimension rather than being a general national story without a specific community focus.

Examples of Investigative Ideas

The fellowship description provides examples of investigations that have demonstrated the type of reporting the program seeks to support.

One example involved a reporter at The Baltimore Banner who had reason to believe that Baltimore’s overdose crisis was the worst in the nation.

Another involved journalists at Mississippi Today who had evidence of abuses in local sheriffs’ offices.

A further example involved a reporter at The Desert Sun in Palm Springs, California, who suspected a pattern of deaths inside local jails.

These examples illustrate the importance of starting with a specific reporting lead, evidence or pattern and then developing it through deeper investigation.

Applicants should therefore avoid presenting only a broad topic. Instead, they should explain what they suspect, what evidence they have already encountered, what remains unknown and what further reporting could establish.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit several materials as part of their application.

The New York Times specifically requires applicants to upload their:

  • Résumé.
  • Cover letter.
  • Five published reporting clips.

These materials must be submitted in one attachment, and applications that do not follow the required instructions or fail to include the necessary materials will not be considered.

The five clips should demonstrate the applicant’s journalistic ability and should help editors assess the applicant’s experience and reporting style.

Cover Letter and Investigative Story Pitch

The cover letter is a particularly important component of the application.

Applicants must include at least one investigative story idea or pitch, although they may include more than one if they wish.

Each story idea or pitch should be limited to 500 words.

The New York Times states that applicants do not need to submit polished, publication-ready pitches. Instead, the purpose of the questions is to help editors understand the applicant’s reporting process and determine what kinds of editorial assistance, resources and support could help develop the investigation.

Questions Applicants Should Address

A proposed investigation should address the following areas:

1. What is the investigative story idea?

Applicants should clearly describe the issue they want to investigate.

They should also explain what the investigation could reveal that is not already known.

The applicant should consider:

  • What is the central allegation, question or problem?
  • What evidence currently exists?
  • What new information could the investigation uncover?
  • Why is the issue important to the community?

2. Who Has Been Harmed?

Applicants should identify the people or communities affected by the issue.

They should explain:

  • Who experienced harm?
  • What form did the harm take?
  • How extensive is the harm?
  • What evidence demonstrates the harm?
  • Why is the harm significant?

This section should demonstrate that the applicant understands the human consequences of the issue rather than viewing the investigation solely as an institutional or abstract problem.

3. Who Should Be Held Accountable?

Applicants should identify the relevant individuals, organizations or institutions that have responsibility or authority.

They should explain:

  • Who has the power to influence the situation?
  • What decisions or actions are relevant?
  • What failures or conduct require examination?
  • How could the reporting establish accountability?

4. What Records, Data and Sources Are Needed?

Investigative reporting frequently requires extensive documentation.

Applicants should identify the critical materials that would be necessary to pursue their investigation, which could include:

  • Government records.
  • Public records.
  • Court documents.
  • Financial records.
  • Internal documents.
  • Public databases.
  • Government datasets.
  • Corporate records.
  • Emails or correspondence.
  • Interviews with affected individuals.
  • Expert sources.
  • Former employees.
  • Current employees.
  • Community members.

Applicants should also explain how they have obtained, or could obtain, these sources.

5. What Support Is Needed?

Applicants should identify the obstacles preventing them from fully pursuing the investigation independently.

These barriers might involve:

  • Lack of time.
  • Limited newsroom resources.
  • Insufficient editorial support.
  • Difficulty obtaining records.
  • Data analysis requirements.
  • Legal or reporting challenges.
  • Geographic limitations.
  • The need for additional reporting resources.
  • Difficulty accessing important sources.

The application should make clear why the Local Investigations Fellowship would be useful for advancing the investigation.

6. What Has Already Been Reported?

Applicants should demonstrate awareness of existing journalism on their proposed subject.

They should explain:

  • What other journalists have already reported.
  • What is already known.
  • What important questions remain unanswered.
  • How the proposed investigation could add new information.

Applicants should also include notable reporting clips related to the subject where appropriate.

Five Published Clips Required

Applicants are expected to submit five published clips that demonstrate excellence in journalism.

The clips should showcase abilities such as:

  • Evocative writing.
  • High-impact news reporting.
  • Investigative reporting.
  • Strong storytelling.
  • Community-focused reporting.
  • Effective use of sources.
  • Ability to explain complex issues clearly.
  • Ability to highlight the experiences and voices of local communities.

Applicants should upload the full text of their clips, rather than submitting links alone.

Choosing the appropriate clips is therefore an important part of the application. Candidates should select work that demonstrates their strongest reporting and provides evidence of their ability to pursue meaningful local journalism.

Work Authorization Requirements

The Local Investigations Fellowship has a specific U.S. work authorization requirement.

Applicants must be authorized to work in the United States.

The New York Times states that it will not sponsor new work visas for the fellowship.

However, applicants who already hold an existing work visa may be considered. The organization may also consider candidates holding a valid student visa that can be extended through Optional Practical Training (OPT).

This requirement is particularly important for international journalists because meeting the professional qualifications alone does not establish eligibility if the applicant does not have the required authorization to work in the United States.

Fellowship Duration and Location

The Local Investigations Fellowship is a one-year program.

Although the job listing is categorized as remote within the United States, fellows will be based in the communities where their investigations are taking place. The fellowship also includes periodic trips to The New York Times offices for training and support.

This structure allows fellows to remain close to the people, institutions and communities they are reporting on while still receiving direct editorial support from experienced investigative journalists.

Compensation

The listed annual base pay for the position is:

$85,262.84 USD per year

The job listing states that the annual base pay range for this role is $85,262.84–$85,262.84 USD.

For U.S. roles, eligible employees may also receive additional compensation depending on the role, including variable compensation such as an annual bonus and restricted stock.

Benefits

Depending on eligibility and the specific role, benefits may include:

  • Medical insurance.
  • Dental insurance.
  • Vision benefits.
  • Flexible Spending Accounts (FSAs).
  • Company-matching 401(k) plan.
  • Employee stock purchase plan.
  • Paid vacation.
  • Paid sick days.
  • Paid parental leave.
  • Tuition reimbursement.
  • Professional development programs.

The exact benefits available to an individual fellow may depend on applicable employment terms and eligibility.

Application Frequency

Candidates may apply to the Local Investigations Fellowship once per calendar year.

Applicants may also apply for other newsroom opportunities at The New York Times, but they must submit a separate application for each program.

This means candidates interested in multiple opportunities should ensure that they complete the required application materials for each individual position rather than assuming one application will automatically be considered for multiple programs.

Application Deadline

No fixed application deadline is provided in the job listing.

Applicants are notified about their status on a rolling basis. The New York Times notes that the fellowship is highly competitive and receives a high level of interest.

Candidates should therefore review the official listing and application portal for the current status of the opportunity before applying.

The organization also states that it will not accept applications submitted by mail or email. Applications must be submitted through the official application process.

How Applicants Are Selected

The New York Times states that applicants will be notified on a rolling basis.

The organization does not promise to acknowledge every application immediately or provide status updates to every applicant throughout the vetting process.

Candidates may be contacted for interviews as needed.

Because the fellowship receives substantial interest, applicants should ensure that their submission clearly communicates their reporting experience, investigative idea, evidence, sources, community impact and understanding of the subject.

Important Note About Generative AI

The New York Times includes specific instructions concerning generative artificial intelligence in its hiring process.

Candidates are asked to submit their own work and not use generative AI tools to generate substantive content during the application and interview process.

Applicants should therefore carefully follow the organization’s instructions and ensure that submitted reporting clips, pitches and other substantive application materials comply with the stated requirements.

Union Representation

The position is represented by the NewsGuild of New York.

This is an employment-related condition identified in the official listing.

Equal Opportunity and Inclusion

The New York Times Company states that it is committed to maintaining a diverse workforce with people from different backgrounds and experiences.

The organization states that it is an Equal Opportunity Employer and that it does not discriminate based on legally protected characteristics, including sex, age, race, color, creed, national origin, religion, marital status, pregnancy, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, disability, genetic characteristics, citizenship, veteran or military status and other characteristics protected by law.

The company also states that reasonable accommodations will be provided as required by applicable federal, state and local laws.

Applicants seeking an accommodation during the application or interview process can contact the organization’s designated accommodations email address listed in the official vacancy announcement.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants interested in this fellowship should approach the application as an investigative journalism proposal rather than a conventional employment application.

1. Develop a Specific Investigation

Avoid submitting a proposal that is too broad.

Instead of simply proposing to investigate an issue such as public housing, policing, healthcare or local government, identify a specific question, pattern, failure or allegation that can be investigated through evidence.

2. Demonstrate What Is Already Known

Research the subject thoroughly and identify existing reporting.

A strong application should show that the applicant understands the current state of knowledge and can explain what their proposed investigation would add.

3. Identify the Evidence

Think beyond interviews.

Consider what records, data, documents and other evidence could establish the facts of the investigation.

4. Establish the Human Impact

Explain how the issue affects real people and communities.

Demonstrate the consequences of the situation and identify people who can provide firsthand accounts.

5. Establish Accountability

An investigative story should have a clear accountability component.

Applicants should identify the institutions or individuals whose actions, decisions or failures are relevant to the investigation and explain how evidence could establish responsibility.

6. Select Strong Reporting Clips

The five clips should collectively demonstrate the applicant’s strongest journalism.

Applicants should choose published work that shows their ability to report accurately, write clearly, develop sources and tell stories that matter to local communities.

7. Be Specific About Reporting Challenges

If the investigation requires resources that the applicant’s current newsroom or freelance work cannot provide, explain exactly what is needed.

This could include additional time, data analysis, records research, editorial guidance, travel or other reporting resources.

APPLY HERE

Important Fraud Warning

Applicants should be cautious about fraudulent job advertisements and fake employment offers.

The New York Times states that legitimate job opportunities are accessible through its official careers website. The company also states that it will not ask applicants for financial information or payment and will not direct applicants to third parties to obtain employment.

Applicants should never send money to someone claiming that payment is required to secure a position at The New York Times.

Anyone who encounters a suspected fraudulent job posting or offer can report it to The New York Times using the contact information provided in the official listing. The organization also directs applicants to relevant government fraud-reporting channels.

Visit HERE to learn more about the The New York Times Local Investigations Fellowship 2026.

Conclusion

The New York Times Local Investigations Fellowship provides experienced local journalists with a structured opportunity to spend a year pursuing an important investigative story with the support of veteran investigative editors. The fellowship is centered on producing meaningful local journalism that can uncover new information, establish accountability and give communities a clearer understanding of issues affecting their lives.

Applicants should pay particular attention to the investigative story proposal, as the application requires them to explain what they want to investigate, what they hope to uncover, who has been harmed, who may be accountable, what records and sources will be needed, what barriers they face and how existing reporting relates to their proposed work.

With a one-year duration, editorial mentorship, investigative reporting support and the opportunity for the resulting work to be published by The New York Times, the fellowship is structured for journalists who already possess professional reporting experience and have a significant local investigation they want to pursue.

Applicants should carefully review the official vacancy information, confirm that they meet the U.S. work authorization requirements and prepare all required materials before submitting their application.

item.content:encoded:
The Umholi we Africa (UwA) Fellowship Cohort 5 is inviting applications from exceptional young African professionals who are committed to public service, governance, policymaking, and ethical leadership.

The fully funded, 12-month fellowship is designed to provide a practical pathway for talented African professionals to contribute to government and public-sector work in their home countries. Selected fellows are placed in strategic roles where they can work alongside ministers, members of parliament, and senior public-sector leaders, gaining firsthand experience in governance, policymaking, institutional transformation, and national development.

The fellowship is delivered by AL for Governance and Africa Career Networks, in partnership with the Mastercard Foundation. A particularly important eligibility requirement is that applicants must be graduates of either the African Leadership Academy (ALA) or the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program.

Applications for Cohort 5 opened on 4 September 2026 and will close on 31 October 2026.

About the Umholi we Africa Fellowship

The Umholi we Africa Fellowship is a leadership pathway focused on developing the next generation of African public leaders.

The fellowship seeks to connect highly capable young African professionals with practical opportunities inside government and policy institutions. Rather than limiting leadership development to classroom-based learning, the programme combines hands-on public-sector experience, leadership development, mentorship, coaching, and exposure to policymaking.

During the 12-month fellowship, fellows serve in their home countries and contribute to the work of public leaders and institutions. Their responsibilities may involve research, policy analysis, data collection, project management, strategic planning, communications, stakeholder engagement, and other activities related to public-sector work.

The programme is intended for professionals who are interested in building long-term careers in governance, public service, policy, or political leadership.

What Does “Umholi we Africa” Mean?

The fellowship’s name, Umholi we Africa, reflects its broader leadership mission across the African continent.

The programme is designed around the idea of developing young African professionals who can contribute to public institutions and national development.

Through practical experience and leadership development, fellows are exposed to the realities of public-sector work while developing the skills and networks required to contribute to governance and policy processes.

Who Organizes the Fellowship?

The Umholi we Africa Fellowship is associated with:

  • AL for Governance
  • Africa Career Networks
  • Mastercard Foundation

The programme is part of a broader effort to create pathways for young African professionals into governance and public leadership. The AL for Governance network focuses on developing ethical public leaders, strengthening connections among young professionals, and encouraging intergenerational mentorship.

What Do Umholi we Africa Fellows Do?

Selected fellows are placed in strategic roles supporting public leaders and institutions in their respective home countries.

Their work can cover a wide range of governance and policy functions.

1. Policy Research and Analysis

Fellows may conduct research and collect information needed to support government or policy work.

This can include:

  • Conducting background research
  • Collecting and analyzing data
  • Supporting policy analysis
  • Preparing research findings
  • Providing evidence for policy discussions
  • Supporting strategic advisory activities

This experience can give fellows practical exposure to how research and evidence are used in public decision-making.

2. Strategic Advisory Support

Fellows may support senior public leaders with strategic tasks and decision-support activities.

Depending on their placement, this could involve preparing background information, conducting research, developing briefing materials, or helping public leaders understand relevant issues.

3. Project Planning and Management

The fellowship can also expose participants to practical project management within government or policy institutions.

Fellows may assist with:

  • Project planning
  • Implementation
  • Budgeting
  • Monitoring
  • Evaluation
  • Progress tracking
  • Reporting

This provides an opportunity to understand how public-sector initiatives move from planning to implementation.

4. Policy Briefs and Reports

Written communication is another important part of the fellowship.

Fellows may contribute to the preparation of:

  • Policy briefs
  • Reports
  • Speeches
  • Briefing documents
  • Communication materials
  • Strategic documents

These responsibilities can help participants strengthen their ability to communicate complex policy and development issues clearly.

5. Stakeholder Engagement

Fellows may participate in stakeholder consultations, community engagement, and public outreach.

This can provide exposure to the different groups involved in policymaking and public-sector implementation.

6. Communications

Depending on their placement, fellows may support public-sector communication activities and prepare materials used to communicate policies, initiatives, or institutional priorities.

7. Leadership Development

The programme does not only provide workplace experience.

Fellows also participate in leadership training, mentorship, coaching, and professional development through the AL for Governance network.

Fellowship Duration

The Umholi we Africa Fellowship is a 12-month programme.

During this period, selected fellows combine practical work in public-sector or policy environments with leadership development and mentorship.

The fellowship therefore provides an extended period in which participants can gain experience rather than participating in a short-term leadership event or workshop.

Where Will Fellows Work?

The fellowship places selected participants in their home African countries.

Fellows work with public leaders and institutions in their respective countries, allowing them to gain experience within their own national governance and policy environments.

This home-country placement model means that the programme is intended to help participants contribute to national development while developing careers within African public-sector and policy ecosystems.

Fully Funded Fellowship

The Umholi we Africa Fellowship is described as a fully funded programme.

The opportunity combines funding with practical professional experience, leadership development, mentorship, and coaching.

The available announcement does not provide a detailed breakdown of every financial component or the monetary value of the fellowship. Applicants should therefore consult the official application information for the precise terms of the funding package.

Who Can Apply for the Umholi we Africa Fellowship?

The fellowship has specific eligibility requirements, and meeting the basic requirements is important before beginning an application.

Applicants must meet the following criteria:

1. Be an African National

Applicants must be nationals of an African country.

The fellowship is therefore intended for young African professionals and is not a general worldwide fellowship.

2. Be an ALA or Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program Graduate

This is a particularly important eligibility condition.

Applicants must be graduates of either:

  • African Leadership Academy (ALA), or
  • Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program

This means that being an African professional alone is not sufficient to meet the stated eligibility requirements.

3. Hold at Least a University Degree

Applicants must have completed at least a university degree.

4. Have at Least Four Years of Professional Experience

Applicants must have a minimum of four years of professional experience.

This makes the fellowship particularly relevant to established young professionals rather than recent university graduates with limited work experience.

5. Demonstrate Commitment to Public Service

Applicants should demonstrate a genuine commitment to public service and ethical leadership.

6. Demonstrate Interest in Governance and Policy

The programme is looking for applicants with a demonstrated interest in:

  • Governance
  • Policymaking
  • Public leadership
  • Political leadership
  • Institutional transformation
  • Civic engagement

7. Aspire to a Public Leadership Career

Applicants should have an aspiration to pursue political, policy, or public leadership roles.

The fellowship is designed for people who want to contribute to governance and public institutions rather than simply seeking general professional development.

Click HERE to read more.

Skills and Qualities Sought

In addition to the formal eligibility requirements, the fellowship information identifies several qualities that applicants should demonstrate.

These include:

  • Strong analytical skills
  • Research capabilities
  • Interpersonal skills
  • Commitment to ethical leadership
  • Interest in public service
  • Interest in governance and policymaking
  • Civic engagement
  • Commitment to institutional transformation
  • Leadership potential
  • Professionalism
  • Accountability
  • Innovation

Applicants should therefore make sure their application demonstrates not only what they have achieved professionally but also how their experience connects to governance and public service.

What Applicants Should Highlight

Eligible applicants should ensure that their application clearly communicates their professional experience and their interest in public leadership.

Relevant areas to demonstrate may include:

Professional Experience

Explain the responsibilities, projects, leadership roles, and achievements gained through at least four years of professional experience.

Leadership Experience

Highlight situations where you have taken responsibility, led teams, managed projects, solved problems, or contributed to organizational change.

Public-Service Motivation

Explain why public service matters to you and how your professional experience connects to broader societal needs.

Governance and Policy Interest

Demonstrate your understanding of governance or policy issues and explain why you want to develop a career in this area.

Analytical and Research Skills

Provide evidence of your ability to conduct research, analyze information, interpret data, and develop evidence-based recommendations.

Long-Term Goals

Clearly explain how the fellowship fits into your longer-term professional aspirations in governance, policy, or public leadership.

Important Eligibility Check Before Applying

Because the fellowship has a specific alumni requirement, applicants should verify this before investing significant time in the application.

The key eligibility combination is:

African nationality + ALA or Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program graduate + university degree + at least four years of professional experience + demonstrated commitment to public service/governance.

Meeting only some of these conditions does not necessarily establish eligibility.

Important Facts at a Glance

Feature Details
Programme Umholi we Africa Fellowship
Cohort Cohort 5
Duration 12 months
Funding Fully funded
Geographic scope Africa
Placement Fellow’s home African country
Focus Governance, public service, policy and leadership
Application opening 4 September 2026
Application deadline 31 October 2026
Evaluation January–February 2027
Pre-Fellowship Training June 2027
Minimum education University degree
Professional experience Minimum 4 years
Special alumni requirement ALA or Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program graduate
Nationality requirement African national

How to Apply

Eligible applicants should use the official Umholi we Africa Fellowship application process provided by Africa Career Networks and carefully review the current requirements before submitting their application.

The official fellowship information identifies the application deadline as:

31 October 2026

Applicants should verify the latest application instructions, required documents, and submission procedures through the official programme page before applying.

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The Umholi we Africa Fellowship Cohort 5 is a fully funded, 12-month leadership programme designed to create a pathway for qualified young African professionals into governance, public service, policymaking, and public leadership.

The fellowship combines direct experience within government and policy institutions with leadership training, mentorship, coaching, and professional development. Fellows can contribute to research, policy analysis, strategic planning, project management, communications, stakeholder engagement, and other activities supporting public leaders and institutions.

Click HERE for more fellowship opportunities.

item.content:encoded:
The Center for Empirical Research in Economics and Behavioral Sciences (CEREB) at the University of Erfurt, Germany, is inviting applications from outstanding prospective doctoral researchers for PhD scholarships beginning in 2027. The scholarships are funded through the Thuringian State Graduate Support Programme and are intended to support excellent doctoral projects undertaken within the University of Erfurt’s structured doctoral environment. University of Erfurt

This opportunity is particularly suitable for researchers whose academic interests lie at the intersection of economics, psychology, behavioral sciences, management, organizational research, decision-making, health communication, corporate governance, business ethics, and related empirical disciplines.

Successful applicants can receive €1,400 per month, with additional family support where applicable. The standard funding period is three years, with the possibility of an extension for a fourth year upon application. The application deadline is 24 November 2026 at 11:59 p.m. CET. University of Erfurt

About the University of Erfurt CEREB

The Center for Empirical Research in Economics and Behavioral Sciences, commonly known as CEREB, is an interdisciplinary graduate and research center based at the University of Erfurt.

Its central aim is to bring together theoretical approaches and empirical research methods to investigate important questions about:

  • human behavior;
  • individual and collective decision-making;
  • economic behavior;
  • psychological processes;
  • organizational decision-making;
  • institutional environments;
  • education and life-course development; and
  • social outcomes.

CEREB places particular emphasis on understanding how people make decisions, why they make particular choices, how those choices can be empirically studied, and how better decision-making can be facilitated in different social and institutional settings. University of Erfurt

The center brings together researchers from different academic disciplines and career stages and operates within an internationally connected research environment.

What Does CEREB Research?

CEREB’s academic profile is strongly interdisciplinary. Research combines theoretical models of human behavior with quantitative and empirical approaches.

The center examines decision-making across a broad spectrum, including conventional concepts of rational choice as well as more complex behavioral models involving:

  • bounded rationality;
  • heuristics;
  • context-dependent decisions;
  • social influences;
  • individual differences;
  • organizational structures;
  • institutional processes; and
  • life-course development.

Researchers also study how people pursue goals, how different environments affect their choices, and how institutional arrangements influence both individual and managerial decision-making. University of Erfurt

University of Erfurt CEREB PhD Scholarships 2027

CEREB is currently seeking excellent PhD candidates who would undertake doctoral research at the University of Erfurt with financial support from a university-administered doctoral scholarship.

The wider funding call states that the University of Erfurt intends to award up to four doctoral scholarships using funding from the Thuringian State Graduate Support Programme.

The awards are designed to support high-quality doctoral projects conducted within the University’s structured Erfurt Doctoral and Postdoctoral Programme (EPPP) through one of its certified Graduate Centres or the Max-Weber-Kolleg. University of Erfurt

Applicants interested specifically in CEREB must align their doctoral project with CEREB’s academic and research areas.

Research Areas Available Through CEREB

Successful CEREB scholarship recipients may have opportunities to interact and collaborate with researchers working in several fields, including:

  • Behavioral economics
  • Social psychology
  • Health psychology
  • Organizational psychology
  • Organization and management
  • Corporate ethics
  • Business ethics
  • Corporate governance
  • Individual decision-making
  • Group decision-making
  • Child decision-making
  • Medical decision-making
  • Health communication

The broad interdisciplinary structure allows doctoral researchers to develop projects spanning more than one academic discipline, provided there is a clear conceptual and methodological connection to CEREB’s research profile. University of Erfurt

Scholarship Funding

The CEREB-related doctoral scholarship provides substantial financial support for selected doctoral candidates.

Monthly Scholarship

Successful applicants receive:

€1,400 per month

as the basic scholarship amount. University of Erfurt

Family Allowance

Scholarship recipients with dependent children may also qualify for an additional family allowance.

The current funding structure provides:

  • €300 per month for the first dependent child
  • €150 per month for each additional dependent child

This additional support is provided on top of the monthly scholarship amount. University of Erfurt

Research and Travel Support

Subject to the availability of funding, doctoral scholarship holders may also apply for support toward research-related expenses.

Up to:

€600 per funding year

may be available for approved research materials and travel expenses. University of Erfurt

This could potentially support activities connected with the doctoral project, such as academic travel, research materials, conferences, fieldwork, or similar research-related requirements, subject to approval and applicable funding rules.

Scholarship Duration

The standard doctoral scholarship period is:

Three years

However, scholarship recipients may request an extension for:

One additional year

which means the overall funding period can potentially reach a maximum of four years. University of Erfurt

An extension is not necessarily automatic and is subject to the applicable scholarship rules and approval process.

Funding Start Date

The planned start of scholarship funding is:

1 April 2027

The University specifies that funding must begin no later than:

1 July 2027. University of Erfurt

Applicants should therefore plan their doctoral admission, university enrolment, Graduate Centre membership, and other administrative requirements accordingly.

Benefits of Joining CEREB

The scholarship is more than a monthly financial award. Successful researchers become part of a structured academic environment intended to support doctoral training, research development, professional networking, and academic career advancement.

Scholarship recipients can benefit from:

Structured Graduate Programme

Candidates have access to a structured graduate programme within the University of Erfurt.

This provides a more organized doctoral experience compared with undertaking research completely independently.

Research Network

CEREB brings together scholars from economics, psychology, management and behavioral sciences, giving doctoral candidates access to interdisciplinary research expertise.

International Academic Connections

CEREB maintains collaborations with international research institutions and encourages academically rigorous, internationally connected research. University of Erfurt

Research Projects

Doctoral candidates may become connected with recent and ongoing research projects relevant to the center’s areas of expertise.

Academic Skills Training

The University also provides scholarship holders with access to Academic Skills Training, designed to strengthen research and professional competencies.

Science Communication Opportunities

Scholarship holders may participate in university platforms supporting the communication of scientific research to wider audiences. University of Erfurt

Responsibilities of Scholarship Holders

Successful recipients are expected to participate actively in the University’s structured doctoral environment.

Scholarship holders are generally required to:

  • participate regularly in the programme of their Graduate Centre or the Max-Weber-Kolleg;
  • complete at least six Academic Skills Training courses;
  • participate actively in academic networking activities; and
  • submit a progress report approximately 18 months after funding begins. University of Erfurt

Applicants should therefore view the scholarship as participation in a structured research programme rather than simply receiving financial assistance.

Academic Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must demonstrate strong academic qualifications and clear research potential.

The official funding requirements include above-average academic achievements and examination results demonstrating particular aptitude for academic research. University of Erfurt

The selection process particularly considers:

  • previous academic performance;
  • examination results;
  • previous academic or research work;
  • research potential;
  • methodological quality of the proposed doctoral project;
  • academic significance of the research;
  • quality of the research proposal; and
  • feasibility of the proposed work and time schedule. University of Erfurt

Applicants should therefore submit a carefully designed PhD proposal that demonstrates both academic significance and practical feasibility.

Acceptance as a Doctoral Candidate

Applicants must be accepted as doctoral candidates by:

  • one of the University of Erfurt’s faculties; or
  • the Max-Weber-Kolleg,

by the beginning of the funding period at the latest.

That doctoral status must then be maintained throughout the scholarship period. University of Erfurt

For CEREB applicants, the proposed doctoral project would normally be associated with the relevant University of Erfurt faculty and CEREB research structure.

University Enrolment Requirement

Scholarship recipients must also be formally enrolled, or matriculated, at the University of Erfurt by the start of the funding period.

Doctoral enrolment is therefore distinct from simply receiving the scholarship or securing the support of a potential supervisor. University of Erfurt

CEREB Membership Requirement

Applicants whose scholarship application is assigned to CEREB must obtain full membership of the relevant Graduate Centre no later than the beginning of the funding period.

Applicants will also need evidence that they have established contact with their intended Graduate Centre during the application process. University of Erfurt

Importantly, the official scholarship documentation states that candidates cannot apply simultaneously to several Graduate Centres.

Applicants must therefore identify the Graduate Centre most appropriate for their proposed research.

Health Insurance Requirement

Successful candidates must provide current proof of health insurance by the beginning of the scholarship funding period. University of Erfurt

International candidates should therefore take health insurance requirements into account while preparing for doctoral study in Germany.

Restrictions on Double Funding

The scholarship generally cannot be combined with another source of public funding that covers the same period and purpose.

The University specifies that simultaneous funding from other public funds or publicly financed institutions for the same purpose is not permitted. University of Erfurt

Funding for research-related stays abroad may nevertheless remain possible where permitted under the applicable regulations.

Employment During the Scholarship

Scholarship holders can undertake limited paid employment, but restrictions apply.

Paid research or teaching work at a university or non-university research institution is permitted for up to:

12 hours per week

Other employment is generally limited to:

5 hours per week.

Participation in teaching must also remain within the University’s prescribed limits. University of Erfurt

Applicants who intend to continue substantial employment alongside their PhD should therefore review these conditions carefully before applying.

Application Documents Required

The University requires candidates to submit a comprehensive doctoral scholarship application.

1. Cover Letter

Applicants must submit a cover letter of no more than two pages.

It should identify the Graduate Centre to which the applicant is applying and provide detailed reasons for seeking the scholarship through that particular Graduate Centre.

For this opportunity, applicants would identify CEREB where appropriate.

The letter may also explain:

  • why CEREB is appropriate for the proposed doctoral research;
  • links between the applicant’s research interests and CEREB;
  • any relevant connections with other University research areas;
  • whether work on the doctoral project has already started; and
  • the extent of any preparatory research already undertaken. University of Erfurt

2. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit:

  • a CV in tabular format; and
  • the University’s supplementary CV form.

Applicants should clearly present academic qualifications, research experience, publications, professional experience where relevant, methodological training and other achievements supporting their doctoral research potential.

3. PhD Research Proposal

A detailed exposé of the proposed doctoral project is required.

The research proposal should include:

  • the main research question;
  • background and current state of research;
  • research objectives;
  • proposed methodology; and
  • bibliography.

The main project outline should normally be approximately 6–8 pages, excluding the cover page and bibliography. University of Erfurt

4. Work and Time Schedule

Applicants must provide a detailed plan explaining how the PhD will be completed within the standard three-year scholarship period.

A credible timeline is an important part of the evaluation because the selection committee assesses the plausibility and feasibility of the proposed work schedule.

5. Evidence of Contact With CEREB

Applicants must submit confirmation showing that contact has been established with the relevant Graduate Centre.

Applicants who are already full members may instead provide the appropriate Graduate Centre admission documentation. University of Erfurt

6. Doctoral Acceptance Confirmation

Where already available, applicants should include confirmation from the relevant University faculty or the Max-Weber-Kolleg showing that they have been accepted as a doctoral candidate.

7. Academic Publications and Presentations

Applicants who have publications, conference papers or academic presentations may provide a list of these achievements.

While not every applicant will necessarily have extensive publications, relevant academic work may strengthen the application.

8. University Degree Certificates

Applicants must submit relevant degree certificates.

This can include:

  • Diploma;
  • Magister;
  • Bachelor’s degree; and
  • Master’s degree.

Where documents were originally issued in a language other than German or English, applicants must also provide a certified translation into German or English. University of Erfurt

9. Final Thesis

Applicants must provide a complete copy of their relevant final academic thesis, such as a:

  • Master’s thesis;
  • Diploma thesis; or
  • Magister thesis.

If the thesis was not written in German or English, applicants must additionally provide a summary of up to two pages in German or English. University of Erfurt

10. Data Processing Consent

Applicants must submit the required signed consent regarding processing of personal data.

11. Academic Recommendation Letter

A current and signed academic recommendation is also required.

The recommendation must be written by a:

  • professor; or
  • other university teacher,

either at the University of Erfurt or another higher education institution. University of Erfurt

Importantly, the recommendation must not be included in the applicant’s main application PDF.

The referee must submit it separately and before the application deadline.

How to Submit the Application

Applicants must combine the required documents, except the separately submitted recommendation letter, into:

One PDF file

The PDF must:

  • include a table of contents;
  • contain documents in the prescribed order; and
  • not exceed 5 MB. University of Erfurt

Applications are submitted by email only to the University of Erfurt’s Research and Graduate Services.

The required email subject format is:

Application for the State Graduate Scholarship 2026 – surname, first name

Incomplete applications, applications failing to meet formal requirements, or submissions received after the deadline cannot be considered. University of Erfurt

Application Deadline

The final application deadline is:

24 November 2026 at 11:59 p.m. CET

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day because the application requires coordination with a Graduate Centre and an academic referee.

Funding is expected to begin on 1 April 2027, or no later than 1 July 2027. University of Erfurt

Selection Process

Applications will be evaluated primarily on the applicant’s academic capabilities and the quality of the proposed doctoral project.

The selection committee considers:

  • academic achievements;
  • examination results;
  • previous scholarly work;
  • demonstrated research ability;
  • quality of the proposed doctoral research;
  • methodological rigor;
  • academic relevance;
  • feasibility of the research plan; and
  • realism of the proposed timetable. University of Erfurt

The University expects the application evaluation and decision process to take approximately ten weeks, with applicants expected to receive results by around the end of February 2027. University of Erfurt

The final number of scholarships depends on the availability and allocation of state funding.

Equal Opportunity and International Applicants

The University states that applications are welcomed regardless of origin, gender, disability, age, religion or worldview, sexual orientation or identity. University of Erfurt

There is no nationality restriction stated in the official scholarship announcement.

Therefore, qualified international candidates may apply, provided they satisfy the academic, doctoral admission, Graduate Centre membership, enrolment and other applicable requirements.

Where candidates have equivalent qualifications and projects of comparable quality, the University’s selection framework also addresses gender equality and may consider circumstances including disability, chronic illness, voluntary engagement and certain social criteria. Providing such personal information is voluntary. University of Erfurt

Why Consider the CEREB PhD Scholarship?

For students interested in empirical research on economics and human behavior, the CEREB scholarship provides several significant advantages.

It combines:

  • monthly financial support;
  • multi-year doctoral funding;
  • possible family allowances;
  • potential research and travel support;
  • structured doctoral training;
  • interdisciplinary research supervision;
  • interaction with researchers from multiple fields;
  • academic skills development;
  • international research connections; and
  • participation in an established German research university.

The interdisciplinary nature of CEREB may be particularly valuable for applicants whose research cannot be comfortably classified within a single traditional discipline.

Researchers studying economic decisions, psychology, management, organizational behavior, governance, health communication or human decision-making may therefore find the center particularly relevant.

Important Advice for Applicants

Applicants should begin preparations well before the November deadline.

A strong application is likely to require several separate components to be developed simultaneously.

Candidates should particularly focus on:

  1. identifying whether their doctoral topic genuinely fits CEREB’s research profile;
  2. establishing contact with CEREB before applying;
  3. developing a rigorous and realistic research proposal;
  4. identifying an appropriate potential doctoral supervisor;
  5. obtaining an academic recommendation early;
  6. preparing degree certificates and certified translations where required;
  7. ensuring the doctoral project can realistically be completed within three years; and
  8. checking every formal application requirement before submission.

A technically strong proposal that is poorly matched with CEREB may be less competitive than a project demonstrating clear intellectual overlap with the center’s research agenda.

Conclusion

The University of Erfurt CEREB PhD Scholarships 2027 offer an excellent opportunity for high-performing prospective doctoral researchers seeking structured PhD training in Germany in areas connected with economics, psychology, behavioral sciences, management, decision-making and organizational research.

With funding of €1,400 per month, additional family allowances, possible research and travel funding, structured academic training and potential support for up to four years, the programme provides a strong foundation for researchers pursuing an academic or research-intensive career.

Applicants should pay particular attention to the quality of their doctoral research proposal, methodological design, academic record and fit with CEREB’s interdisciplinary research agenda.

The application deadline is 24 November 2026 at 11:59 p.m. CET, with funding scheduled to begin from 1 April 2027. University of Erfurt
